Nickel-Catalyzed Reductive 1,4-Alkylacylation of 1,3-Enynes
Enabling Synthesis of Allenyl Ketones
Quanyuan Wang, Keyi Peng, Xiangyuan Yao, Yuezhou Yuan, Ya Chen,* and Guo-Jun Deng*

ABSTRACT: A nickel-catalyzed reductive 1,4-alkylacylation of 1,3-enynes has been established using nonactivated tertiary alkyl
bromides and aromatic anhydrides as dual electrophiles. This protocol enables efficient assembly of tetrasubstituted allenyl ketones
with high chemo- and regioselectivity. Mechanistic insights reveal the radical relay process involving the synergistic interactions of
nickel and zinc. The allenyl ketone products serve as modular building blocks, particularly for constructing fully carbon-substituted
furans via Au-catalyzed cycloisomerization with selective 1,2-aryl migration, enhancing the synthetic practicality.
T
he allenyl ketone scaffold, prevalent in natural products
and bioactive molecules,
1
has emerged as a versatile
synthon in synthetic chemistry due to its unique combination
of allenyl and carbonyl moieties.
2
This structural motif
demonstrates remarkable utility in diverse high-value trans-
formations, including nucleophilic additions,
3
cycloadditions,
4
and cycloisomerization reactions,
5
particularly for constructing
polysubstituted furans.
6
Despite its synthetic utility, traditional
approaches rely either on stepwise functionalization of
preformed allenes (e.g., oxidation of allenols or nucleophilic
additions to allenyl esters) or on carbonyl allenylation using
highly prefunctionalized substrates such as α-alkynyl/β-
chlorovinyl ketones,
7
which demand multistep preparations
and face challenges in functional group compatibility. More-
over, these methods frequently require stoichiometric oxidants
or moisture-sensitive organometallic reagents yet remain
ineffective for constructing fully substituted allenyl ketones
(Scheme 1a). To overcome these synthetic limitations, a one-
pot strategy that can simultaneously introduce both the allenyl
and ketocarbonyl units from simple starting materials is
urgently needed.
Recent years have witnessed significant advances in radical-
mediated 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes,
8
enabling
efficient access to multisubstituted allenes bearing cyano,
9
aryl,
10
alkynyl,
11
and halo groups.
12
In contrast, the catalytic
synthesis of allenyl ketones via radical 1,4-difunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes remains underdeveloped (Scheme 1b). Notable
research by Du, Huang and Li demonstrated NHC-catalyzed
1,4-alkylacylation through allenyl-ketyl radical cross-cou-
pling,
13
albeit limited to activated radical precursors like alkyl
halides, redox ester, ring-strained oxime esters and Togni
reagent due to NHC’s constrained reducing power. Subse-
quent work by Zhang and Wang achieved 1,4-sulfonylacylation
and fluoroalkylative acylation with sulfinates and acyl fluorides
via NHC/photoredox dual catalysis.
14
Concurrently, Kong’s
group achieved 1,4-alkylacylation via synergistic photocata-
lyzed hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and nickel catalysis,
15
though requiring large excesses of saturated hydrocarbons as
radical precursors. Most recently, Wu and Guo independently
established palladium- and nickel-catalyzed four-component
1,4-alkylcarbonylation using the CO insertion strategy.
16
Despite these remarkable advances, it is still desirable to
explore modular strategies enabling the efficient assembly of
structurally diverse, fully substituted allenyl ketones from
bench-stable feedstocks.
The nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling paradigm has driven
transformative advances in alkene/alkyne difunctionalization,
17
with recent extensions to 1,3-enynes demonstrating excep-
tional site selectivity. Notably, Rueping’s and our independent
studies established electrochemical and photochemical 1,4-
alkylarylation of 1,3-enynes through a synergistic merger of
nickel catalysis with radical chemistry,
18
successfully leveraging
nonactivated alkyl bromides as bench-stable precursors.
Following these seminal works, subsequent contributions
from Hong, He and Wei further advanced this paradigm.
19

Capitalizing on these developments and driven by our
persistent interest in difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes,
20
we
hypothesized that multicomponent reductive cross-electrophile
reactions could be a good strategy to realize 1,4-alkylacylation
of 1,3-enynes from readily accessible materials with straightfor-
ward operational procedures. Key challenges lay in controlling
chemo-/regioselectivity amidst competing pathways (two-
component couplings, hydroalkylation, and 1,2-/3,4-difunc-
tionalization). Herein, we disclose a nickel-catalyzed reductive
1,4-alkylacylation of 1,3-enynes using nonactivated tertiary
alkyl bromides and acid anhydrides, delivering tetrasubstituted
allenyl ketones with high efficiency and selectivity (Scheme
1c).
The model reaction employing 1,3-enyne (1a), tert-butyl
bromide (2a) and benzoic anhydride (3a) as substrates was
systematically investigated to establish optimal conditions.
Following evaluation of reaction solvents, catalysts, and
additives (see the Supporting Information for details), the
desired product 4a was successfully obtained in 51% isolated
yield under the conditions: NiBr
2
·DME (10 mol %) as catalyst,
dtbbpy (12 mol %) as ligand, zinc powder (4.0 equiv) as
reducing agent, LiBr (2.0 equiv) as additive in DMAc under
nitrogen atmosphere at 40 °C for 12 h (Table 1, entry 1).
Control experiments revealed the essential roles of four critical
components: nickel catalyst, ligand, reductant, and additive
(entries 2−4). Subsequent additives further screening demon-
strated that while NaBr, LiCl and MgCl
2
could partially
substitute LiBr, these alternatives provided diminished yields
(42−46%) (entry 5). Ligand evaluation showed the indis-
pensable role of the dtbbpy ligand, as substitutions with
phenanthroline or triphenylphosphine resulted in drastic yield
reductions (entry 6). Intriguingly, catalyst optimization studies
identified NiCl
2
·DME as the most effective catalyst, achieving
64% yield compared to significantly lower efficiencies with
NiBr
2
, NiCl
2
or NiI
2
(22−49%) (entries 7−8). Furthermore,
alternative reductants (Mn, Mg, or Fe powder) proved to be
completely ineffective, highlighting the unique effectiveness of
zinc powder in facilitating this transformation (entry 9).
Building upon the optimized conditions, we subsequently
explored the structural versatility of 1,3-enynes in this catalytic
system (Scheme 2). Initial investigations focused on the
electronic effects of C-2 aryl substituents, revealing that
substrates containing para-substituted electron-donating
groups and electron-withdrawing halogens all underwent
smooth transformation to afford products 4a-4g with
comparable efficiencies (63−68% yield). However, upon

replacement of the ester group, the reaction led to a decreased
yield (4h), accompanied by the formation of a certain amount
of hydroalkylation byproducts. Further examination of steric
influences demonstrated that meta- or ortho-substituted
substrates with methoxy or methyl groups (4i-4j) maintained
satisfactory reactivity, indicating remarkable tolerance toward
steric hindrance in this catalytic protocol. Notably, the
extension of the C-2 aryl group to 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl
(4k) led to a diminished yield. When heterocyclic systems,
such as 1,3-benzodioxolyl and thiophene, were applied, the
desired products were obtained with moderate yields (4l-4m).
Studies on C-4 substituents showed effective compatibility
with both linear alkyl chains (4n, 4o) and branched alkyl
groups (4p, 4q), delivering the target products in acceptable
yields. However, the reaction proved intolerant to extreme
steric bulk, as evidenced by complete inhibition with tert-butyl
or trimethylsilyl substituents, ascribed to the inaccessibility of
the metal catalytic center.
Subsequently, scope exploration of tertiary alkyl bromides
was conducted under the optimized conditions (Scheme 3).
The systematic evaluation revealed that short-chain aliphatic
tertiary alkyl bromides (5a-5b) and the cyclohexyl-substituted
analogue (5c) led to obviously decreased yields, attributed to
competing β-hydride elimination pathways. Pleasingly, increas-
ing the equivalents of these substrates significantly enhanced
the yields to synthetically useful levels. Tertiary alkyl bromides
bearing benzyl and phenethyl groups at the central carbon
maintained moderate reactivity, delivering the corresponding
products 5d and 5e in 53% and 56% yields, respectively.
Significantly, the protocol exhibited exceptional tolerance
toward aryl-carboxylic-acid-derived tertiary alkyl bromides
(5f-5l). Electronic modulation with electron-donating (Me,
OMe) and -withdrawing (F, Cl) substituents afforded products
5f-5j in 45−68% yields. Of particular note, heterocyclic
integration with thiophene (5k, 70% yield) or furan (5l, 60%
yield) achieved good efficiency, further confirming the broad
substrate generality of this methodology.
Furthermore, the substrate generality of aromatic anhydrides
was also examined (Scheme 4). Regarding electronic effects,
para-substituted benzene rings bearing electron-donating alkyl
groups (tert-butyl, methyl; 6a-6b) and electron-withdrawing
halogens (F, Cl; 6f-6g) could all be efficiently converted into
desired products with 50−67% yields. Intriguingly, the
methoxy-substituted analogue displayed a drastic yield
reduction (6e), which was attributed to the competitive
hydroalkylation pathway. Further investigation revealed that
the substitution position of substituents on the benzene ring
exhibited no significant influence on the efficiency. Both meta-
and orthomethyl substituents delivered comparable yields (6c-
6d). Notably, extension to polycyclic systems also proved
feasible. The target product 6h was obtained in moderate yield
when the naphthalene-derived substrate was employed. In
contrast, replacing aromatic anhydrides with aliphatic anhy-
drides, such as propionic or isobutyric anhydrides, led to only
trace amounts of the target allenone compounds, as evidenced
by GC-MS analysis.
The scalability of this methodology was confirmed through a
gram-scale synthesis of model product 4a, which retained a
58% yield (5.0 mmol scale, Scheme 5). To showcase the
synthetic versatility, a series of derivatization studies of allenyl
ketones were conducted. Chemoselective reduction with
NaBH
4
under mild conditions cleanly afforded secondary
alcohol 7a (86%) without compromising the allene integrity.

Grignard addition (PhMgBr) efficiently constructed congested
tertiary alcohol 7b in 94% yield. Notably, Wittig olefination
successfully achieved conjugated extension of the allene
skeleton, delivering vinyl-substituted allenyl derivative 7c
with a near-quantitative yield. The gold-catalyzed cyclo-
isomerization with selective 1,2-aryl migration demonstrated
significant synthetic value, enabling efficient access to
tetrasubstituted furans (7d and 7e)�privileged scaffolds in
heterocyclic chemistry.
5
The structure of compound 7e was
unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallography.
A series of control experiments were conducted to clarify the
reaction mechanism. Radical clock studies employing allyl
ether as a probe substrate afforded cyclized product 8a in 27%
yield, confirming radical intermediacy through characteristic
ring-closing pathways (Scheme 6a). Subsequent trapping
studies with 1,1-diphenylethylene selectively captured tert-
butyl radicals (8b, 25% GC yield), while control experiments
with benzoic anhydride revealed no detectable benzoyl radical
adducts (8c/8c′), establishing the involvement of alkyl radical
species (Scheme 6b). Notably, tert-butyl radical generation
persisted without LiBr (8b, 30% GC yield), excluding LiBr’s
participation in radical initiation. Removing the nickel catalyst
and ligand unexpectedly enhanced the formation of 8b (39%
GC yield), demonstrating that zinc-mediated reductive
cleavage of the C−Br bond serves as the predominant radical
source. However, we could not exclude the competent
reductive cleavage of tert-butyl bromide with a low-valence
nickel complex (Scheme 6c). Furthermore, the model reaction
employing 10 mol % Ni(COD)
2
as a catalyst afforded product
4a with 42% isolated yield, whereas no product was observed
with stoichiometric Ni(COD)
2
in the absence of zinc powder
(Scheme 6d). These observations indicate that Ni(0)
preferentially undergoes irreversible oxidative addition with
benzoic anhydride,
21
forming a thermodynamically stable
Ni(II)-benzoyl complex that deactivates alkyl bromide
activation, thereby interrupting the catalytic cycle.
Based on the above mechanistic evidence and precedent
literature,
22
a plausible catalytic cycle is proposed in Scheme
6e. Initiation involves Zn-mediated reduction, generating
active Ni(0) species A, which engages in oxidative addition
with benzoic anhydride 3 to form Ni(II)-acyl complex B.
Concurrently, tert-butyl bromide 2 undergoes single-electron
transfer (SET) mediated by zinc or low-valent nickel species,
liberating a tertiary alkyl radical that participates in
regioselective Giese addition to 1,3-enyne 1. The resultant
propargyl radical undergoes rapid allenyl radical equilibration
via resonance stabilization. The allenyl radical interception by
Ni(II)-acyl complex B produces Ni(III) intermediate C, which
undergoes facile reductive elimination to deliver allenyl ketone
4, while generating Ni(I) species D. Finally, Zn-mediated
single-electron reduction regenerates Ni(0) catalyst A, thereby
completing the catalytic cycle.
In summary, we have reported a nickel-catalyzed reductive
cross-electrophile coupling strategy enabling 1,4-alkylacylation
of 1,3-enynes with nonactivated tertiary alkyl bromides and
aromatic anhydrides. This operationally simple method
features high chemoselectivity and precise regiocontrol while
circumventing conventional dependencies on moisture-sensi-
tive organometallic reagents or toxic CO gas. Preliminary
mechanistic studies reveal a synergistic nickel−zinc catalytic
cycle involving radical generation from alkyl bromides and the
oxidative addition of anhydrides. The protocol demonstrates
gram-scale compatibility and a good functional group
tolerance. Strategic derivatizations of the allenyl ketone
products, including gold-catalyzed cycloisomerization with
selective 1,2-aryl migration, enable the streamlined synthesis
of fully carbon-substituted furans.

Nickel-Catalyzed Reductive 1,4-Alkylacylation of 1,3-Enynes
Enabling Synthesis of Allenyl Ketones
Quanyuan Wang, Keyi Peng, Xiangyuan Yao, Yuezhou Yuan, Ya Chen,* and Guo-Jun Deng*

ABSTRACT: A nickel-catalyzed reductive 1,4-alkylacylation of 1,3-enynes has been established using nonactivated tertiary alkyl
bromides and aromatic anhydrides as dual electrophiles. This protocol enables eficient assembly of tetrasubstituted allenyl ketones
with high chemo- and regioselectivity. Mechanistic insights reveal the radical relay process involving the synergistic interactions of
nickel and zinc. The allenyl ketone products serve as modular building blocks, particularly for constructing fully carbon-substituted
furans via Au-catalyzed cycloisomerization with selective 1,2-aryl migration, enhancing the synthetic practicality.

structurally diverse, fully substituted allenyl ketones from
bench-stable feedstocks.

A series of control experiments were conducted to clarify the
reaction mechanism. Radical clock studies employing allyl
ether as a probe substrate aforded cyclized product 8a in 27%

ring-closing pathways (Scheme 6a). Subsequent trapping

studies with 1,1-diphenylethylene selectively captured tert-
butyl radicals (8b, 25% GC yield), while control experiments
with benzoic anhydride revealed no detectable benzoyl radical
adducts (8c/8c′), establishing the involvement of alkyl radical
species (Scheme 6b). Notably, tert-butyl radical generation
persisted without LiBr (8b, 30% GC yield), excluding LiBr’s
participation in radical initiation. Removing the nickel catalyst
and ligand unexpectedly enhanced the formation of 8b (39%
GC yield), demonstrating that zinc-mediated reductive
cleavage of the C−Br bond serves as the predominant radical
source. However, we could not exclude the competent
reductive cleavage of tert-butyl bromide with a low-valence

nickel complex (Scheme 6c). Furthermore, the model reaction
employing 10 mol % Ni(COD) as a catalyst aforded product
4a with 42% isolated yield, whereas no product was observed
with stoichiometric Ni(COD) in the absence of zinc powder
(Scheme 6d). These observations indicate that Ni(0)
preferentially undergoes irreversible oxidative addition with
benzoic anhydride,<sup>21</sup> forming a thermodynamically stable
Ni(II)-benzoyl complex that deactivates alkyl bromide
activation, thereby interrupting the catalytic cycle.

Based on the above mechanistic evidence and precedent
literature,<sup>22</sup> a plausible catalytic cycle is proposed in Scheme
6e. Initiation involves Zn-mediated reduction, generating
active Ni(0) species A, which engages in oxidative addition
with benzoic anhydride 3 to form Ni(II)-acyl complex B.
Concurrently, tert-butyl bromide 2 undergoes single-electron
transfer (SET) mediated by zinc or low-valent nickel species,
liberating a tertiary alkyl radical that participates in
regioselective Giese addition to 1,3-enyne 1. The resultant
propargyl radical undergoes rapid allenyl radical equilibration
via resonance stabilization. The allenyl radical interception by
Ni(II)-acyl complex B produces Ni(III) intermediate C, which
undergoes facile reductive elimination to deliver allenyl ketone
4, while generating Ni(I) species D. Finally, Zn-mediated
single-electron reduction regenerates Ni(0) catalyst A, thereby
completing the catalytic cycle.

In summary, we have reported a nickel-catalyzed reductive
cross-electrophile coupling strategy enabling 1,4-alkylacylation
of 1,3-enynes with nonactivated tertiary alkyl bromides and
aromatic anhydrides. This operationally simple method
features high chemoselectivity and precise regiocontrol while
circumventing conventional dependencies on moisture-sensi-
tive organometallic reagents or toxic CO gas. Preliminary
mechanistic studies reveal a synergistic nickel−zinc catalytic
cycle involving radical generation from alkyl bromides and the
oxidative addition of anhydrides. The protocol demonstrates
gram-scale compatibility and a good functional group
tolerance. Strategic derivatizations of the allenyl ketone
products, including gold-catalyzed cycloisomerization with
selective 1,2-aryl migration, enable the streamlined synthesis
of fully carbon-substituted furans.
